items.stem: Define the term 'merger'.
items.answer: An agreement by two businesses to combine into a single business, usually with the agreement of both sets of shareholders and managers.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, an agreement by two businesses to combine into a single business, usually with the agreement of both sets of shareholders and managers. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a merger and a takeover.
items.answer: In a merger two firms agree to combine as equals; in a takeover one firm buys a controlling interest in another, which may be hostile.
items.markingKey: 1 mark merger = agreed combination; 1 mark takeover = purchase of >50% of shares / control. [2]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why a business might choose a joint venture rather than a takeover.
items.answer: A joint venture needs less capital and shares risk; it allows the partners to keep their independence and avoids paying a takeover premium; it can be easier to unwind.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark reason, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Inflation in Turkey has been above 40% for two years. Bosphorus Home AŞ, a public limited company in Turkey with about 3,500 employees, makes washing machines, fridges and ovens sold in Europe and the Middle East. Explain the possible benefits to Bosphorus Home of a horizontal merger with a competitor.
items.answer: Points to develop for Bosphorus Home: horizontal integration combines firms at the same stage; economies of scale lower unit costs; higher market share and pricing power; removes a rival and duplicated costs.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: horizontal integration combines firms at the same stage. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Bosphorus Home: household appliance manufacturing, about 3,500 employees, public limited company in Turkey; inflation in Turkey has been above 40% for two years). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Bosphorus Home, e.g. economies of scale lower unit costs; higher market share and pricing power; removes a rival and duplicated costs. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Tejo Mobility SA is a public limited company based in Lisbon, Portugal. It assembles electric scooters and e-bikes for sale across the European Union and employs about 600 people. Battery supply problems from Asia have delayed several large orders. Explain why a takeover of a foreign rival might fail to increase the profits of Tejo Mobility.
items.answer: Points to develop for Tejo Mobility: takeovers often destroy value; overpaying through a large takeover premium; clash of corporate cultures lowers motivation; diseconomies of scale and integration costs.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: takeovers often destroy value. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Tejo Mobility: vehicle manufacturing, about 600 employees, public limited company in Portugal; battery supply problems from Asia have delayed several large orders). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Tejo Mobility, e.g. overpaying through a large takeover premium; clash of corporate cultures lowers motivation; diseconomies of scale and integration costs. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Demand has grown faster than its small brewery can produce. Cape Brew Co. (Pty) Ltd, a private limited company in South Africa with about 140 employees, brews craft beers and low-sugar soft drinks sold through bars and supermarkets. Explain the possible benefits to Cape Brew of a horizontal merger with a competitor.
items.answer: Points to develop for Cape Brew: horizontal integration combines firms at the same stage; economies of scale lower unit costs; higher market share and pricing power; removes a rival and duplicated costs.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: horizontal integration combines firms at the same stage. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Cape Brew: beverages, about 140 employees, private limited company in South Africa; demand has grown faster than its small brewery can produce). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Cape Brew, e.g. economies of scale lower unit costs; higher market share and pricing power; removes a rival and duplicated costs. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Clients are starting to replace human call handlers with artificial intelligence. IslaConnect Inc., a private limited company in the Philippines with about 2,600 employees, runs customer-service call centres for banks and airlines in the USA and Australia. Recommend whether IslaConnect should enter Canada through a joint venture or by setting up its own subsidiary.
items.answer: For: a joint venture shares cost and risk; local partner knowledge; faster entry. Against: a subsidiary keeps full control and profit; protects know-how; avoids partner conflict. Judgement: the decision for IslaConnect depends mainly on how well it understands Canada, and also on its available finance.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [2]: uses case evidence (IslaConnect: business process outsourcing, about 2,600 employees, private limited company in the Philippines; clients are starting to replace human call handlers with artificial intelligence). AO3 Analysis [4]: arguments for, e.g. a joint venture shares cost and risk; local partner knowledge; faster entry; arguments against, e.g. a subsidiary keeps full control and profit; protects know-how; avoids partner conflict. AO4 Evaluation [4]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on how well it understands Canada; its available finance; the legal rules on foreign ownership. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to IslaConnect, not a generic one. [12]

Judgement: the decision for Siam Ready Meals depends mainly on how well it understands South Korea, and also on its available finance.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [3]: relevant concepts/theory. items.stem: Nile Pharma plc is a public limited company based in Cairo, Egypt. It manufactures generic medicines for hospitals and pharmacies in Africa and the Middle East and employs about 1,800 people. Most of its raw ingredients are imported and paid for in US dollars. Explain one advantage to Nile Pharma of forming a joint venture with a local firm in East Africa.
items.answer: Shares the cost and risk of entry.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant advantage, e.g. shares the cost and risk of entry; gains local market knowledge and contacts; may overcome rules on foreign ownership. 1 mark: explained in the context of Nile Pharma (pharmaceuticals). [2]

items.stem: Explain why a merger may lead to diseconomies of scale.
items.answer: The larger firm may suffer communication problems, slower decisions, poor coordination and lower motivation, raising average costs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named diseconomy; 1 mark how it raises unit cost. [2]

items.stem: Cape Brew Co. (Pty) Ltd plans to take over Lagos Bites Ltd, which has 20 million shares trading at $2.40. To win control it offers a 40% premium. Calculate the offer price per share and the total cost of buying all the shares.
items.answer: $3.36 per share; total $67,200,000

It grows cut flowers and green beans and exports them by air to supermarkets in Europe and employs about 850 people. Its largest European customer has just demanded lower prices and proof of sustainable water use. Explain why a takeover of a foreign rival might fail to increase the profits of Savanna Fresh, and judge which point is most important for Savanna Fresh.
items.answer: Points to develop for Savanna Fresh: takeovers often destroy value; overpaying through a large takeover premium; clash of corporate cultures lowers motivation; diseconomies of scale and integration costs.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: takeovers often destroy value. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Savanna Fresh: horticulture, about 850 employees, private limited company in Kenya; its largest European customer has just demanded lower prices and proof of sustainable water use). items.stem: Based in Cape Town, Cape Brew Co. (Pty) Ltd (private limited company) brews craft beers and low-sugar soft drinks sold through bars and supermarkets. The business has around 140 employees. Demand has grown faster than its small brewery can produce. (a) Define 'joint venture'. (b) Explain one advantage to Cape Brew of taking over one of its suppliers.
items.answer: (a) Two or more businesses agree to share capital, risks and profits in a new, separately managed project or business. (b) Secures supplies of key inputs.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark partial, 2 marks full definition [2] (b) 1 mark point (secures supplies of key inputs; captures the supplier's profit margin; more control over quality and delivery), 1 mark explanation, 1 mark application to Cape Brew [3]

items.stem: Define the term 'economies of scale'.
items.answer: Reductions in a firm's average (unit) costs of production that result from an increase in the scale of operation.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, reductions in a firm's average (unit) costs of production that result from an increase in the scale of operation. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain how technical economies of scale reduce average costs.
items.answer: Large firms can afford specialised, high-capacity machinery and production lines whose high fixed cost is spread over a very large output.
items.markingKey: 1 mark large/specialist equipment; 1 mark fixed cost spread over more units. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a very large business may suffer from lower employee motivation.
items.answer: Workers feel remote from senior managers and their contribution seems small, communication is slow and impersonal, so they feel undervalued.
items.markingKey: 1 mark distance/alienation; 1 mark effect on motivation/productivity. [2]

items.stem: Its biggest customer, a convenience-store chain, wants deliveries twice a day. Siam Ready Meals Co. Ltd, a private limited company in Thailand with about 1,100 employees, produces chilled and frozen ready meals for supermarkets and convenience stores. Explain the diseconomies of scale Siam Ready Meals might experience if it doubles in size.
items.answer: Points to develop for Siam Ready Meals: diseconomies raise average cost at large scale; longer chains of command slow decisions; coordination problems between departments or sites; lower motivation and higher labour turnover.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: diseconomies raise average cost at large scale. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Siam Ready Meals: food manufacturing, about 1,100 employees, private limited company in Thailand; its biggest customer, a convenience-store chain, wants deliveries twice a day). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Siam Ready Meals, e.g. longer chains of command slow decisions; coordination problems between departments or sites; lower motivation and higher labour turnover. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: The owners want to double the number of cafés within three years. Café Cordillera SAS, a private limited company in Colombia with about 900 employees, roasts coffee and runs a chain of 60 cafés. Explain how Café Cordillera could benefit from economies of scale as it grows.
items.answer: Points to develop for Café Cordillera: economies of scale reduce average cost as output rises; purchasing economies on inputs for roasted coffee and café meals; technical and financial economies; lower unit costs allow lower prices or higher margins.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: economies of scale reduce average cost as output rises. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Café Cordillera: food and drink retail, about 900 employees, private limited company in Colombia; the owners want to double the number of cafés within three years). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Café Cordillera, e.g. purchasing economies on inputs for roasted coffee and café meals; technical and financial economies; lower unit costs allow lower prices or higher margins. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.answer: Points to develop for BatikPay: diseconomies raise average cost at large scale; longer chains of command slow decisions; coordination problems between departments or sites; lower motivation and higher labour turnover.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: diseconomies raise average cost at large scale. items.stem: Bosphorus Home AŞ is a public limited company based in Istanbul, Turkey. It makes washing machines, fridges and ovens sold in Europe and the Middle East and employs about 3,500 people. Inflation in Turkey has been above 40% for two years. Evaluate whether Bosphorus Home should aim to become much larger in order to gain economies of scale.
items.answer: For: lower unit costs and better margins; stronger bargaining power; more funds for research and marketing. Against: diseconomies of scale; loss of flexibility and customer focus; demand may not support larger output. Judgement: the decision for Bosphorus Home depends mainly on the size of the market for household appliances, and also on how well its management can control a larger organisation.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Bosphorus Home, not a generic one. [12]

Online sales are growing quickly while sales in its high-street stores are falling. Evaluate whether Iberia Moda should aim to become much larger in order to gain economies of scale.
items.answer: For: lower unit costs and better margins; stronger bargaining power; more funds for research and marketing. Against: diseconomies of scale; loss of flexibility and customer focus; demand may not support larger output. Judgement: the decision for Iberia Moda depends mainly on the size of the market for fast-fashion clothing, and also on how well its management can control a larger organisation.

items.stem: Based in Bangkok, Siam Ready Meals Co. Ltd (private limited company) produces chilled and frozen ready meals for supermarkets and convenience stores. The business has around 1,100 employees. Its biggest customer, a convenience-store chain, wants deliveries twice a day. Explain one disadvantage to Siam Ready Meals of doubling its scale of production.
items.answer: Communication and coordination problems.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant disadvantage, e.g. communication and coordination problems; lower staff motivation; risk of overcapacity if demand does not grow. 1 mark: explained in the context of Siam Ready Meals (food manufacturing). [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between internal and external economies of scale.
items.answer: Internal economies come from the growth of the firm itself (e.g. bulk buying); external economies come from the growth of the industry or area (e.g. specialist suppliers locating nearby).
items.markingKey: 1 mark internal; 1 mark external with example. [2]

items.stem: Maple Learning Inc. has monthly fixed costs of $800,000 and variable costs of $5 per unit. Calculate the average cost per unit at outputs of 25,000 and 75,000 units. At the higher output, bulk buying cuts variable cost by 15%. Calculate the new average cost at 75,000 units.
items.answer: $37.00 and $15.67; $14.92 with the discount

items.stem: Based in Jakarta, Nusantara Apparel Tbk (public limited company) makes sportswear under contract for global brands. The business has around 4,000 employees. A global brand has threatened to cancel its contract after a report on long working hours. (a) Define 'external economies of scale'. (b) Analyse the diseconomies of scale Nusantara Apparel might experience if it doubles in size.
items.answer: (a) Reductions in average cost that a firm gains from the growth of its whole industry or area, e.g. a pool of skilled labour or specialist suppliers nearby. (b) Diseconomies raise average cost at large scale; longer chains of command slow decisions; coordination problems between departments or sites; lower motivation and higher labour turnover.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark partial, 2 marks full definition [2] (b) AO1 Knowledge [2]: diseconomies raise average cost at large scale. AO2 Application [2]: answer uses the case (Nusantara Apparel: clothing manufacturing, about 4,000 employees, public limited company in Indonesia; a global brand has threatened to cancel its contract after a report on long working hours). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Nusantara Apparel, e.g. longer chains of command slow decisions; coordination problems between departments or sites; lower motivation and higher labour turnover. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [6]

items.stem: Define the term 'globalisation'.
items.answer: The growing integration of the world's economies through increased trade, movement of capital, people, ideas and technology across borders.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, the growing integration of the world's economies through increased trade, movement of capital, people, ideas and technology across borders. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why a business may decide to become a multinational.
items.answer: To be closer to foreign customers and avoid tariffs and transport costs; to use cheaper labour or resources; to spread risk across several economies.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark reason, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Explain one potential disadvantage to a host country of a large MNC operating there.
items.answer: Profits may be sent back to the home country, local firms may be forced out, and the MNC may exploit weak labour or environmental laws.
items.markingKey: 1 mark disadvantage; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: Shareholders are pressing for higher dividends while engineers want more spending on research. Lumen Robotics plc, a public limited company in Singapore with about 2,400 employees, designs and builds robots used on factory assembly lines. Explain the possible impact on the economy of Singapore if a large foreign MNC built a factory competing with Lumen Robotics.
items.answer: Points to develop for Lumen Robotics: FDI creates jobs and raises incomes; technology and skills spill over to local firms; local firms such as Lumen Robotics face stronger competition; profits may be repatriated.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: FDI creates jobs and raises incomes. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Lumen Robotics: industrial engineering, about 2,400 employees, public limited company in Singapore; shareholders are pressing for higher dividends while engineers want more spending on research). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Lumen Robotics, e.g. technology and skills spill over to local firms; local firms such as Lumen Robotics face stronger competition; profits may be repatriated. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Bookings are highly seasonal and most guides are employed only for the summer. Kiwi Trails Ltd, a private limited company in New Zealand with about 90 employees, runs guided hiking, kayaking and cycling tours. Explain how increasing globalisation is likely to affect Kiwi Trails.
items.answer: Points to develop for Kiwi Trails: globalisation integrates world markets; new export opportunities for adventure tours; more intense competition from overseas firms; access to global supply chains, but more exposure to disruption.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: globalisation integrates world markets. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Kiwi Trails: tourism, about 90 employees, private limited company in New Zealand; bookings are highly seasonal and most guides are employed only for the summer). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Kiwi Trails, e.g. new export opportunities for adventure tours; more intense competition from overseas firms; access to global supply chains, but more exposure to disruption. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Demand has grown faster than its small brewery can produce. Cape Brew Co. (Pty) Ltd, a private limited company in South Africa with about 140 employees, brews craft beers and low-sugar soft drinks sold through bars and supermarkets. Evaluate whether Cape Brew should become a multinational by setting up operations in Namibia and Botswana.
items.answer: For: access to a large new market; lower costs or avoiding tariffs; spreads risk across economies. Against: high cost and risk; cultural and legal differences; control and communication difficulties. Judgement: the decision for Cape Brew depends mainly on the size and growth of the market in Namibia and Botswana, and also on political and economic stability there.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Cape Brew, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: Which is a likely benefit to a host country of an MNC opening a factory there?
options: Lower competition for local firms in every case
Guaranteed higher tax revenue in every case
New jobs and transfer of skills and technology
Profits always stay in the host country
items.answer: New jobs and transfer of skills and technology
items.markingKey: New jobs and transfer of skills and technology. FDI brings jobs, training, technology and investment, though profits may be repatriated.

items.stem: Based in Lima, Andes Textil SA (family-owned private company) makes premium alpaca knitwear for fashion retailers in North America and Japan. The business has around 320 employees. The founder is retiring and the new managing director wants to modernise production. Explain one disadvantage to Andes Textil of increasing globalisation of its industry.
items.answer: More foreign competition at home.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant disadvantage, e.g. more foreign competition at home; exposure to exchange-rate risk; pressure on prices and costs. 1 mark: explained in the context of Andes Textil (textile manufacturing). [2]

items.stem: Define the term 'protectionism'.
items.answer: Government measures that restrict imports to protect domestic industries from foreign competition, e.g. tariffs, quotas and subsidies.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, government measures that restrict imports to protect domestic industries from foreign competition, e.g. tariffs, quotas and subsidies. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Which is an example of a protectionist measure?
options: A rise in the minimum wage
items.answer: A 25% tax on imported steel
items.markingKey: A 25% tax on imported steel. A tariff is a tax on imports and protects domestic producers.

items.stem: Explain how a tariff on imported components could affect a domestic manufacturer.
items.answer: The components become more expensive, so unit costs rise; the firm must raise prices or accept lower margins, or switch to domestic suppliers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark higher costs; 1 mark consequence (price/margin/supplier switch). [2]

items.stem: Andes Textil SA is a family-owned private company based in Lima, Peru. It makes premium alpaca knitwear for fashion retailers in North America and Japan and employs about 320 people. The founder is retiring and the new managing director wants to modernise production. Explain the likely effects on Andes Textil if Peru joined a free trade area with its neighbours.
items.answer: Points to develop for Andes Textil: a free trade area removes tariffs between members; larger market for exports; more competition at home; cheaper imported inputs from member countries.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: a free trade area removes tariffs between members. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Andes Textil: textile manufacturing, about 320 employees, family-owned private company in Peru; the founder is retiring and the new managing director wants to modernise production). Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

Bookings are highly seasonal and most guides are employed only for the summer. Discuss whether Kiwi Trails should set up production inside a trade bloc to avoid its common external tariff.
items.answer: For: avoids tariffs and becomes price competitive; closer to customers; tariff-free access to every member. Against: high investment cost and risk; possibly higher labour costs; management of distant operations. Judgement: the decision for Kiwi Trails depends mainly on the size of the tariff, and also on the importance of the bloc's market to sales.

items.stem: Nusantara Apparel Tbk sells a product in Indonesia for $150.00. A similar imported product sells for $120. The government imposes a 25% tariff on imports, which is passed on in full. Calculate the new price of the imported product and the price difference between the two products.
items.answer: $150.00; difference $0.00
items.markingKey: Import price = $120 × 1.25 = $150.00 [1]; difference = $0.00 (import still cheaper) [1]. [2]

items.stem: A chocolate manufacturer takes over a cocoa plantation. What type of integration is this?
items.answer: Backward vertical integration
items.markingKey: Backward vertical integration. Buying a supplier at an earlier stage of production is backward vertical integration.

items.stem: Andina Solar SpA is a private limited company based in Santiago, Chile. It designs and installs solar power systems for farms, mines and homes and employs about 380 people. The government has announced new subsidies for business investment in renewable energy. Explain why a takeover of a foreign rival might fail to increase the profits of Andina Solar.
items.answer: Points to develop for Andina Solar: takeovers often destroy value; overpaying through a large takeover premium; clash of corporate cultures lowers motivation; diseconomies of scale and integration costs.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: takeovers often destroy value. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Andina Solar: renewable energy, about 380 employees, private limited company in Chile; the government has announced new subsidies for business investment in renewable energy). items.stem: Based in Accra, Gold Coast Cocoa Ltd (private limited company) buys cocoa from local co-operatives and makes premium chocolate bars. The business has around 450 employees. World cocoa prices have doubled in eighteen months. Recommend whether Gold Coast Cocoa should enter the United Kingdom through a joint venture or by setting up its own subsidiary.
items.answer: For: a joint venture shares cost and risk; local partner knowledge; faster entry. Against: a subsidiary keeps full control and profit; protects know-how; avoids partner conflict. Judgement: the decision for Gold Coast Cocoa depends mainly on how well it understands the United Kingdom, and also on its available finance.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Gold Coast Cocoa, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: Explain how globalisation increases competition for domestic businesses.
items.answer: Lower trade barriers and cheaper transport let foreign firms sell into the domestic market, so local firms face more rivals on price and quality.

items.stem: Which of the following best defines 'vertical integration'?
options: The growing integration of the world's economies through increased trade, movement of capital, people, ideas and technology across borders.
A merger or takeover with a firm at a different stage of production in the same industry, either backward (towards suppliers) or forward (towards customers).
An agreement by two businesses to combine into a single business, usually with the agreement of both sets of shareholders and managers.
Investment by a business in productive assets (e.g. factories, offices) in another country.
items.answer: A merger or takeover with a firm at a different stage of production in the same industry, either backward (towards suppliers) or forward (towards customers).
items.markingKey: vertical integration: A merger or takeover with a firm at a different stage of production in the same industry, either backward (towards suppliers) or forward (towards customers).
